title: New operator designs for Halpern iterations with explicit rates under Hölder error bounds
question: When many constraints must hold at once, how can we find the feasible solution closest to a given reference point?
idea: A feasibility method can find a point satisfying every constraint without selecting the closest one. Halpern iteration adds a vanishing pull toward the original reference point. This anchor turns a broad family of projection operators into methods for best approximation.
result: We establish convergence to the metric projection and explicit rates for feasibility and distance to that projection under Hölder error bounds. The geometry of the intersection determines the rates.
application: Constrained reconstruction: adjust a noisy estimate as little as possible while enforcing convex consistency constraints. The paper tests best approximation over intersections of ellipsoids and polyhedra.
caption: A two-disk example with T equal to alternating projections. The gold point is the anchor; the path approaches its closest point in the intersection.
sourceNote: Published paper; illustration uses a simple two-dimensional instance.

title: Parallelizing the circumcentered reflection method
question: Can we use several processors to solve affine constraints while preserving the geometry that makes circumcenter methods effective?
idea: Reflect the current point across several affine subspaces independently, then combine those reflected points through their circumcenter: the point in their affine hull equally distant from each. The independent reflection work can run in parallel.
result: For affine subspaces with nonempty intersection, P-CRM converges linearly to the projection of the initial point onto the intersection. Its analysis also compares it with simultaneous projections.
application: Large systems of linear constraints, including projection onto the solution set of a consistent linear system. Groups of equations can be handled independently before the circumcenter combines their information.
caption: Two intersecting lines illustrate the geometry: x and its two reflections lie on a circle centered at the intersection. Higher-dimensional problems generally require repeated steps.
sourceNote: Read the preprint for the full affine-subspace framework.

title: Parallel polyhedral projection method for the convex feasibility problem
shortTitle: Turning curved constraints into useful cuts
question: How can we combine information from many convex constraints in a single productive step?
idea: Project onto the individual sets in parallel. Each projection supplies a supporting half-space containing the feasible intersection. Projecting onto their intersection uses all this local geometric information at once. A3PM allows controlled approximations in these operations.
result: The methods converge globally without a regularity assumption. Error bounds give linear rates, and additional geometric conditions yield superlinear convergence for 3PM.
application: Convex constraint satisfaction in reconstruction and estimation. Different measurements or physical restrictions define separate convex sets; supporting half-spaces provide a tractable outer approximation of their common feasible region.
caption: An exact 3PM step for three disks. Dashed lines support the disks; the shaded polygon contains their intersection. The next iterate is the projection onto that polygon.
sourceNote: The illustration uses exact projections; A3PM additionally supports inexact operations.

title: Deep centralization for the circumcentered reflection method
question: Can a more carefully chosen centralization step make circumcenter updates more effective?
idea: ecCRM replaces a fixed centralization rule with an admissible operator T and a parameter α. A deeper operator composes additional projections before the circumcenter step; a varying α gives another way to control the update.
result: The framework preserves global convergence and linear rates under regularity, with superlinearity under additional smooth geometric assumptions. Matrix-completion and ellipsoid experiments demonstrate the practical value of the operator and parameter choices.
application: Positive-semidefinite matrix completion: recover a matrix that both matches observed entries and satisfies a structural constraint. These are two different sets, so the method can alternate their projections and exploit circumcenter geometry.
formula: Standard: T = PᵧPₓ     Deep: T = PᵧPₓPᵧ
caption: An illustrative rank-two positive-semidefinite matrix and a symmetric observation pattern. Reveal one feasible completion to see how structure fills missing entries; this is not an ecCRM run.
sourceNote: Here “deep” describes a composition of projection operators.

title: FlexGrad: A Root-Free Approach to Adaptive Step Sizes
question: If gradients keep pointing in the same direction, should an adaptive optimizer keep shrinking its steps?
idea: Squared gradients measure magnitude but lose directional information. FlexGrad uses both cumulative gradients and cumulative squared gradients. Persistent directions can support larger steps, while noisy sequences retain AdaGrad-like behavior, without an auxiliary search procedure.
result: For convex Lipschitz objectives, the global and coordinate-wise variants attain the optimal asymptotic rate for nonsmooth convex optimization. Experiments examine convex and nonconvex problems.
application: First-order optimization for machine learning. The method adapts to the gradient information available during training, making directional persistence a useful signal for choosing step sizes.
formula: Directional signal: Σₜ gₜ     Gradient energy: Σₜ gₜ²
caption: Synthetic one-dimensional gradients with equal magnitudes. Switching the sign pattern changes the accumulated direction while leaving the sum of squared gradients unchanged.
sourceNote: This visualization explains the signal; it does not plot training results or optimizer step sizes.

title: Dimension-free complexity guarantees for dual dynamic programming
shortTitle: Learning the cost of future decisions
question: Can we analyze dynamic programming without an iteration bound that grows exponentially with the number of state variables?
idea: Approximate each cost-to-go function from below using affine cuts. The FDDP framework permits flexible model updates, including classical multi-cut models and a memory-efficient variant retaining two cuts per stage. Smoothing and penalization extend the analysis to linearly coupled convex problems.
result: We derive dimension-independent iteration-complexity bounds with the other problem constants held fixed. Individual subproblem solves can still become more expensive as the state dimension increases.
application: Large deterministic planning problems with decisions coupled across stages, such as inventory or resource allocation. A compact model of future cost helps avoid solving the entire horizon as one large problem.
caption: A one-dimensional convex cost-to-go function. Add supporting cuts to improve its lower approximation. This illustrates the cut mechanism shared by DDP models.
sourceNote: The plot illustrates a multi-cut lower model, not the specific two-cut update.

title: Bidirectional SDDP with dimension-free complexity for solving strongly convex stochastic dynamic programming equations
shortTitle: Using repeated scenarios to refine decisions
question: How does strong convexity help us understand the effort needed to make decisions over an uncertain horizon?
idea: BSDDP stores trial points along sampled scenario paths. When a full path is sampled again, the method uses its previous trial points and the current path's realizations to update cost-to-go models before the forward decisions.
result: Under the paper's assumptions, the expected iteration bound for an approximately optimal first-stage decision with optimal recourse is independent of state dimension when the other constants are fixed. Path probabilities and the horizon remain part of the bound.
application: Sequential planning under uncertainty, such as reservoir management or inventory control. A decision today changes tomorrow's state, while future inflows or demand remain uncertain.
formula: Sample a path · Recall its trial points · Refine the models
caption: A toy scenario tree with four full paths. Step through the sample sequence: a repeated path activates a model update using trial points stored at its earlier visit.
sourceNote: The explanation follows the revised manuscript's first-stage guarantee and repeated-full-path mechanism.

title: Tracking Time-Varying Equilibria in Decision-Dependent Stochastic Variational Inequalities
shortTitle: Following an equilibrium that keeps moving
question: What happens when our decisions change the data distribution, and the equilibrium itself changes over time?
idea: A variational inequality describes equilibrium through an operator rather than a single minimization objective. In a decision-dependent model, the choice also affects the distribution generating observations. Time variation adds a moving target to this feedback loop.
result: This project studies how extragradient-type methods track evolving equilibria and how tracking error relates to environmental change. The manuscript is in preparation.
application: Adaptive pricing or deployment of predictive models: actions can influence demand or the population of future observations. Tracking a changing equilibrium can be more relevant than solving one fixed optimization problem.
formula: Find x*ₜ ∈ C: ⟨Fₜ(x*ₜ), x − x*ₜ⟩ ≥ 0 for all x ∈ C
caption: A deterministic toy field Fₜ(x) = x − x*ₜ, tracked by an extragradient update. Increase target drift to explore tracking lag; the full project also considers stochastic and decision-dependent operators.
sourceNote: Research direction; the toy illustration does not assert a theorem from the forthcoming manuscript.

title: Regularized SDDP via trust-region stabilization for multistage stochastic programs
shortTitle: Making early planning steps more stable
question: How can we keep early decisions useful when our approximation of future cost is still rough?
idea: SDDP learns future costs through cutting-plane models. Early models may be inaccurate far from the states already explored. A trust region restricts a trial decision to a neighborhood of a reference point, controlling how far the method moves while those models improve.
result: This project investigates trust-region regularization for multistage stochastic programs. The manuscript is in preparation.
application: Energy scheduling, inventory, and other repeated planning problems in which large swings between trial decisions can make early exploration inefficient. Stabilization gives a way to control that movement.
caption: A toy stage subproblem with a quadratic immediate cost and a cut-based future-cost model. Changing the trust-region radius changes which trial decisions are allowed.
sourceNote: Conceptual illustration of stabilization; results will be described in the forthcoming paper.
